Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a vivid, real-time scene—the protagonist unlocking the door, stepping into the hallway, and opening the jar of hand cream in the bathroom. Grounded in strong sensory details (the click of the lock, the smell of cold dust and roses, the cool texture of the cream), these actions make the moment feel immediate and engaging. Woven seamlessly into this real-time action are brief moments of exposition and summary—such as the memory of how the key needed to be turned, the twenty-year history of her mother's nightly routine with the rose glycerin cream, and her final reflection on the passage of time. This background information is triggered naturally by the physical objects she encounters, enriching the emotional weight of the scene without bogging down the pacing.
